newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Amnesty urges Turkish action on human rights.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty urges Turkish action on human rights.

text.p: Amnesty International accused Turkey's security forces on Thursday of a wide range of rights abuses but said the NATO member country was likely to escape condemnation at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.
At a briefing, the human rights group alleged an increase in disappearances, police torture and extra-judiciary executions in the country.
"We want to see an end to this culture of impunity," said Jonathan Sugden, an Amnesty member investigating Turkish rights abuses.
As a state of strategic importance to the West, Turkey is likely to escape formal condemnation at the Commission despite documented abuses against Kurds, Amnesty officials said.
The European Parliament has blocked aid to Ankara, partly as a result of its shaky human rights, and some European Union politicians have opposed its membership of the 15-nation bloc.
Turkish security forces have cracked down hard in their war with Kurd rebels fighting for independence in the mainly Kurdish southeast, which has claimed 21,000 lives in the past 12 years.
Last week, a U.N. report accused Turkey of a long list of abuses including jailing of writers, torture of journalists, use of force against protesters and routine seizure of newspapers.
Sugden accused the Turkish state of systematic abuses in the southeast and cities. "This is a state within state," he said.

Suspicions over the state's alleged links with organised crime and death squads came to a head in November after a car crash killed a police academy chairman, a wanted gangster and his girlfriend, and seriously injured the former interior minister.
All had been in the same car where police found a cache of guns, silencers, surveillance equipment and traces of cocaine.
The minister, Mehmet Agar, was forced to resign within days of the accident. The dead gangster travelling with him, Abdullah Catli, was wanted for torture and multiple murder.
Catli was also wanted by Interpol for his alleged role in the 1981 assassination attempt on the Pope. In 1990, he escaped from a Swiss prison where he was held for heroin smuggling.
The scandal has shaken Turkey's political establishment. The opposition has supplied evidence that people directed by senior police were involved in killings, extortion and drug smuggling.
